title: Bishop and knight II: from the middle of the board to the edge
summary: Build the net with all three pieces and push the king to the edge.
step.intro: The bishop and knight mate has three stages: drive the king to the edge, get it out of the wrong corner, and mate it in the corner of the bishop's colour. Today is only the first stage, and it is the longest one. Look: the black king sits on e3, right among our pieces, and it wants the marked squares, the centre. On their own, neither the bishop nor the knight can stop it. Together, they can.
step.net: This is the net, the position you need to remember. The bishop on e4 closes the whole diagonal: d5 and f5 belong to it. The knight on d3 covers the squares of the other colour next to that diagonal: c5, e5, f4 and f2. And the white king on e3 plugs what is left, f3 and f4. The black king on g5 has no way back to the centre: every marked square is watched. Seirawan calls this a wall.
step.build1: Let us build the net from scratch, move by move. First the bishop goes to the long diagonal, then the king climbs behind it. Start with the bishop.
step.build1.hint: The bishop wants the a8-h1 diagonal; from g2 it already looks at e4. Then the king climbs, glued to the black king: d2, e3.
step.build1.done: The bishop owns the diagonal and the white king already takes the opposition. Now the knight is missing.
step.build2: The black king is on f5. The knight on c1 does nothing; bring it to the square that covers the dark squares beside the diagonal. Then close the wall with the bishop.
step.build2.hint: The knight goes to d3: from there it watches c5, e5, f4 and f2. And then the bishop goes to e4.
step.build2.done: Net built: bishop on e4, knight on d3, king on e3. Count the squares: the black king cannot get through.
step.push: Once the net is built, the bishop and the knight stay put. The king does the pushing. It advances to d4, then c5 and d5, taking every square the black king gives up, like closing a door behind it. No hurry and no checks.
step.push1: Push with the king. Three moves: d4, c5 and d5.
step.push1.hint: The white king climbs the d-file, always next to the black king: Kd4, then Kc5 and Kd5.
step.push1.done: See where the black king ended up: f6, with the centre behind the white king's back. It has no centre any more.
step.push2: Now the black king runs to the right. Follow with the king: d6, e5 and e6. In the end it only has the back rank.
step.push2.hint: Kd6 takes e7 and e6; Ke5 takes f6 and f5; Ke6 takes f7. Each king move closes one square.
step.push2.done: There it is. The black king is on g8, on the edge, and the first stage is over. Eleven moves and not a single check.
step.defence: Now the other side. The best defence is simple: stay in the centre as long as possible and, when that is no longer possible, run to the wrong corner, the one of the opposite colour to the bishop. Here the bishop is light-squared, so the good corners for us are a8 and h1, and the black king heads for h8. Getting it out of there is the lesson of the W manoeuvre. Today, reaching the edge is enough.
step.traps: Two traps. The first is the pretty check: here Bf5+ looks like it pushes the king, but the black king simply captures the bishop, and without the bishop there is no mate. Before any check, ask whether the piece stays protected. The second is haste: one loose move that opens the net hands the centre back to the king, and the fifty-move rule is counting. Ushenina, world champion at the time, reached this ending in Geneva in 2013 and drew because of it.
step.stalemate: And the third trap, close to the edge: stalemate. Look at this position: the black king on h8 has no move, g8, g7 and h7 are all watched, and it is not in check. Draw. When the king reaches the corner, count its squares before you tighten.
step.summary: Three rules to take with you. One: the bishop closes the diagonal, the knight covers the squares of the other colour beside it and the king plugs the holes. Two: once the net is built, the king does the pushing, taking the square the black king just left. Three: no checks for their own sake, and watch out for hanging pieces and for stalemate.
step.finish: Your turn, against the machine. The net is built. Push the king to the edge and, from there, use what you learned in the W manoeuvre lesson to finish. If you lose the thread, come back and start again: that is how this ending is learned.
ex.e01: White to play. The net is built and the black king stepped back to f6. Which piece makes the next move?
ex.e01.hint: Bishop and knight are already on the right squares. What is missing is the piece that pushes.
ex.e01.solution: The king: Kd4 (Kf4, taking the direct opposition, is just as good). The bishop and the knight stay where they are; the king takes the squares the black king gave up.
ex.e02: White to play. The bishop is already on e4 and the king on e3. Where does the knight join the net?
ex.e02.hint: Look for the square from which the knight watches c5, e5, f4 and f2: the dark squares beside the bishop's diagonal.
ex.e02.solution: Nd3. From d3 the knight covers the dark squares the light-squared bishop cannot reach, and the net closes. Ne2 also works, covering d4 and f4; the king to d4 or f4 is just as fast.
ex.e03: White to play. King on e3, knight on d3, black king on g5. One single move closes the wall.
ex.e03.hint: Which bishop square watches d5 and f5 at the same time?
ex.e03.solution: Be4. This is the lesson's position: with the bishop on e4, c5, d5, e5, f5, f4, f3 and f2 are all watched, and the black king never returns to the centre. Other moves also win, but they let the king wander for a few more moves.
ex.e04: White to play. The black king on c4 wants the centre. Cut it off to the b-file with one move.
ex.e04.hint: The bishop on b2 is on the long diagonal, but behind the king. Bring it to a square from which it takes c5 and c3.
ex.e04.solution: Bd4. The bishop on d4 watches c3 and c5, the knight on d1 watches c3 and e3, the king on e4 watches d3, d4 and d5. The black king is left with b3, b4 and b5: one step from the edge. It is the only move that closes the net at once.
ex.e05: White to play. The black king on g3 tries to come back through f2, f3 or f4. Hold it.
ex.e05.hint: The piece that plugs three squares at once is the king. And careful: Bg4 or Bh3 give the bishop away.
ex.e05.solution: Ke3. Opposition: f2, f3 and f4 belong to the white king, g4 and h3 to the bishop, and the black king only has g2, h2 and h4. Bg4 or Bh3 would be captured by the king.
ex.e06: White to play. The dark-squared bishop cannot reach d3 or d5. Who covers those two squares?
ex.e06.hint: A knight jump that watches d3 and d5 at the same time.
ex.e06.solution: Nf4. From f4 the knight watches d3 and d5, the light squares the bishop on e3 does not cover; the bishop takes d4 and the white king takes b5 and c5. The black king is pushed to b3, b4 or c3, towards the a-file. Bd4 would lose the bishop.
ex.e07: White to play. The black king on b4 is one step from the edge. One king move keeps it there.
ex.e07.hint: Which squares would the black king use to get back to the centre? Take both with the king.
ex.e07.solution: Kd3. The white king takes c3 and c4; the knight on d7 and the bishop on a7 already watch c5 and b6. The black king is stuck on the a- and b-files. Any other move lets the black king out to c4 or c3 and costs many moves.
ex.e08: White to play. Two moves: cut the black king off to the a-file and then hold it there.
ex.e08.hint: First the bishop, to a square that takes b3 and b5 and grabs the a2-g8 diagonal. Then the king takes the opposition.
ex.e08.solution: Bc4, taking b3 and b5: the black king is left with a3, a4 and a5, and it goes to a3. Then Kc3: the white king watches b2, b3 and b4, and the black king is stuck on the a-file. That is the pair of moves that takes you from the net to the edge.
ex.e09: White to play. The black king on c3 is close to your pieces. In three moves, drive it to the a-file: knight, bishop and king, in that order.
ex.e09.hint: Start with a knight check that takes b2 and c1 and leaves the black king without the centre. Then the bishop closes the diagonal and the white king plugs the hole.
ex.e09.solution: Nd3+ forces the king to c4. Bd4 closes the diagonal: c5 and c3 belong to the bishop, and the black king goes to b5. Kd5 takes c5, c6 and c4: only the a-file is left. Three moves, three pieces, and the net closes in one go.
ex.e10: White to play. The black king on c5 wants d4 and d5. In three moves, take the centre away from it: king, knight and bishop.
ex.e10.hint: First the king takes d4. Then the knight looks for a square from which it watches e5 and e7, and the bishop closes the a2-g8 diagonal.
ex.e10.solution: Kc3 takes b4, c4 and d4; the black king goes to d6. Ng6 watches e5 and e7, and the black king comes back to c5. Bc4 closes the diagonal: d5 belongs to the bishop, d4 to the king. The black king has lost the centre and will be pushed to the edge.
key.start: The starting position of the first stage, as shown on Wikipedia (following Seirawan's method): black king among the white pieces.
key.wall: The wall after 5.Be4: bishop on e4, knight on d3 and king on e3. The black king cannot return to the centre. From Wikipedia.
key.centre: Black king in the centre and white pieces in the corner: the whole first stage, from Schnabelwolke's study on Lichess.
key.far: Uncoordinated white pieces and black king on d4, from Gabriel Zárate's study on Lichess: first the king gains space, then bishop and knight form the barrier.
history: Philidor described this mate in his 1749 treatise, L'Analyse des Échecs, and in 1777 drew attention to the knight's route we now call the W manoeuvre. In 1923, Daniel Delétang published in the magazine La Stratégie the triangle method, which shuts the king into smaller and smaller areas. With perfect play, the mate takes at most 33 moves from almost any position, but the ending shows up only once in about six thousand games, which is why many people never study it. The price is high: in 2001, in the Bundesliga, Epishin could not mate Kempinski and the game ended in stalemate; in 2013, in Geneva, Anna Ushenina, world champion at the time, let Girya escape through the fifty-move rule. On the other side, Tal Shaked beat Morozevich with this mate in the penultimate round of the 1997 World Junior Championship and took the title.
practice: Now the real ending, against the clock or without it. Here the black king is already on the edge, on h3, close to the right corner; the rest is up to you. If you want to start from the centre, open the custom training and build the net from scratch.
